chunks.text: Monoon longifolium is an evergreen tree in the custard-apple family (Annonaceae) that can exceed 20 metres in height and is prized above all for its silhouette: a tall, straight central trunk with short, drooping, willowy branches that give the whole tree a neat, pyramidal, almost columnar shape without any pruning. Its long, narrow, lance-shaped leaves have gently wavy margins and pass through a striking colour sequence as they mature, opening coppery-bronze before turning light green and finally a glossy dark green, so a single tree can show three leaf colours at once. The ornamental weeping cultivar sold in nurseries as the 'pendula' form is so densely branched it can look almost leafless at the crown, while an untrimmed wild-type tree grows into a broad, shady canopy tree instead. It is native to southern India and Sri Lanka but has been planted so widely across tropical Asia, East Africa and the Caribbean (it is a common street tree in Jakarta and in Trinidad and Tobago) that many people assume it is native wherever they encounter it. Ecologically it supports two swallowtail butterflies, the tailed jay and the common jay/kite swallowtail, whose caterpillars feed on its leaves, and its small, star-shaped, pale-green spring flowers give way to clusters of 10-20 plum-like fruits that turn purple-black when ripe and are eaten by Asian koels and fruit bats. Because of its dense, year-round foliage it is also commonly planted as a noise and dust screen along roads and institutional boundaries. Historically its light, straight, flexible trunk wood was favoured for ships' masts — which is the direct origin of the common English name 'mast tree' — and is still used today for pencils, boxes, matchsticks and other small turned articles, while seed-oil extracts have been studied in the laboratory for antioxidant and antimicrobial activity, with one mouse study finding only partial, non-curative activity against chloroquine-resistant malaria parasites. The species carries many vernacular names reflecting its long cultivation history across the subcontinent — ashoka in Sanskrit, debadaru in Bengali and Odia, asopalav in Gujarati — and in colonial India it became a favourite planting around churches, cemeteries and government buildings partly because British planters felt it echoed the look of the Mediterranean cypress; this is also the likely source of the alternate name 'cemetery tree'. The IUCN currently lists it as Least Concern. Taxonomically the tree was described in 1782 by Pierre Sonnerat as Uvaria longifolia and spent well over a century classified as Polyalthia longifolia (Sonn.) Thwaites; it was only moved into the segregate genus Monoon, within the tribe Miliuseae, under the combination Monoon longifolium (Sonn.) B.Xue & R.M.K.Saunders following molecular phylogenetic work that split the old, broadly defined Polyalthia into several smaller genera — the Wikipedia article records the renaming but does not itself explain the underlying phylogenetic rationale in detail.

chunks.text: This entry (indexed under the older, still far more widely used name Polyalthia longifolia) reiterates the tree's most persistent point of popular confusion: because of its dense, upright, evergreen habit it is routinely mistaken for the true ashoka tree, Saraca asoca, a completely different and much rarer species with showy orange-red flower clusters that is genuinely sacred in Hindu and Buddhist tradition; Monoon longifolium is therefore better thought of as a convenient, fast-growing, hardy look-alike that has effectively replaced the true ashoka in most modern Indian landscaping precisely because it tolerates pollution, poor soil and drought far better. The page emphasises that the species' popularity as an avenue and compound tree across Indian towns and cities owes less to any religious symbolism of its own and more to practical virtues: it is evergreen year-round, needs almost no pruning to keep a tidy vertical form, grows relatively quickly, and its dense foliage muffles traffic noise and filters roadside dust, which is why it lines so many Indian school, temple and office compounds. It also notes the tree's continued festival use — young sprigs of its leaves are still strung into door and gate garlands (toranas) for Hindu festivals and weddings in parts of India in the same decorative role once filled by mango leaves, a folk use that persists even though botanically it has nothing to do with the sacred ashoka. As with the Wikipedia entry, cautious language is warranted around the medicinal claims circulating for this species online — most derive from small, preliminary phytochemical screening studies rather than established clinical evidence, and should be treated as traditional or experimental uses rather than verified remedies.
